analytic.title: Applying RMA to improve a high-speed, real time data acquisition system

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Unlike other real-time systems, data acquisition applications spend most of their time performing synchronous and asynchronous U 0 operations. This fact, that affects tasks' ability to meet deadlines, can be modelled with some extensions to the classic rate momtonic schedulability test. In this paper we ad* this issue by investigating a case study for the application of rate monotonic analysis to data acquisition systems. We describe a technique for modelling tasks that pedonn asynchronous I/o at the end of their executing perid and we also show the logistic and technical problems that can arise when applying the rate monotonic analysis at different stages during the development process of an application. We illustrate our ideas w i t h a real-time data acquisitian system that we have developed, characterized by a very heterogeneous architecture whose technological components have bten pushed to the limits of their performance and capcity.'

div.head: 1, Introduction
div.p: Rate Monotonic Analysis (RMA) is becoming increasingly popular among the industrial practidoners for predicting the timing behavior of real-time software
There are examples in the literature [l, 41 of schedulability analysis of industrial applications that consist of a set of tasks that share some set of resources.

However, there are few case studies available on the utilization of RMA techniques to guarantee the timing constrains of data acquisition applications. Unlike other systems, when testing the schedulability of these applications the effect of processor utilization is often less important than the impact of the I D blocking time

In this paper we present a case study of the use of RMA in a data acquisition application that has been developed at the CeSATlab of the Autonomous University of Madrid (UAM). This application is a realtime system which is used to inspect industrial containers in order to find early defects in their welds. These metal containers are scanned with a row that carries a set of ultrasonic sensors that acquire the data.

After some sort of transport and processing, this information is displayed in graphical windows and saved to disk in real-time. In a typical inspection. the system acquires as much as 200 GBytes of data at a speed of no less than 1.75 MB/sec.

div.head: Architecture and functional description of the system 2.1 Hardware Architecture
div.p: We can divide the architecture of the system into three main modules: Acquisition Module, Process

Module and Evaluation Module. Although we will only focus on the Process Module for the description of the software architecture and for the application of RMA to improve the system, we present below an overview of the three modules. The Acquisition Module governs the set of ultrasonic sensors that fetch the data. Each sensor is associated with a logical channel, and gathers data by sending ultrasonic pulses and digitizing the resulting echoes. This data is organized in frames and written in a reflective memory board to send them to the F'rocess Module. The reflective memory technology allows different processors to transparently share a region of memory by optic fiber.

The Process Module receives the information of each channel in a corresponding reflective memory board plugged in another V M E chassis. By means of a bus adaptor, this data appears in the address space of a workstation, in which it is buffered, written t o SCSI removable optical disks and displayed in different views in graphical windows. In this manner, the operator can detect in real-time the defects in the welds of the containers.

The sensors of the Acquisition Module are mounted on a robot that scans the container, and that is controlled by a dedicated computer. The Rocess Module receives from this controller the physical coordinates in which the sensors are located at each point of the scanning.
Coordinates are transmitted via a serial line
The Evaluation Module operates off-line and provides a set of powerful tools to analyze the huge amount of data obtained during the inspection.

div.head: Module
div.p: For the objectives of this paper we only need to describe the software architecture of the Process Module. The module consists of the following tasks, ordered by their real-time priority (see FlGURE 1):

getCoord (Task 1). This periodic thread reads the coordinates sent by the robot controller to the serial line of the workstation, and decides which channels must acquire data for that particular physical location. Then. it sends a command to the Acquisition Module through the reflective memory, specifying the channels to be acquired. Finally, this task waits again for the arrival of new coordinates.

readData (Task 2). This thread reads data from the reflective memory to the workstation local memory. Besides buffering the data, it checks if the data buffered up to this moment is enough to Write it to disk efficiently.

If this is the case, it sends a message to the next thread (writeDisk) informing it of the new buffer to dump to disk. It also sends messages to the fourth task (s howD i spl ay) to draw frames in the user display.

writeDisk (Task 3). As explained above, this periodic thread waits for messages of the r e a dD at a, and writes to disks the buffers specified in the messages. This write is performed at the end of the period, using asynchronous I/O calls. The results of this calls are checked for errors at the beginning of next period.

showDisplay (Task4).Finally,thistaskwaits for messages from Task 2 and displays on MOTIF windows the ultrasonic data. From the point of view of real-time priorities, this thread is the less important and can run in background. For this reason, it will not be considered in the rest of the paper.

div.head: Analyzing the temporal behavior of data acquisition systems using RMA
div.p: Data acquisition applications can be modelled as a set of periodic tasks whose goal is to read a certain amount of bytes from a buffer, process them, and write the i n f o " to another storage location. All this has to be done before the associated writer task (the task that writes the buffer from which the reader task reads) fills the buffer.

In the simplest model, the period of the resader task can be the time that it takes for the writer to fill the buffer. If that is the case. the deadline would be equal to the period. However, it is usually better to have the reader task triggered when the buffer is, for instance. one c h i d full. decreasing the period and the deadline to one third of its original amount. Notice that, regarding RMA, this operation is very much the same as the period transformation that sometimes needs to be accomplished to account for the relative importance of tasks when assigning priorities. In data acquisition systems this transformation is useful because with smaller periods, a transient missed deadline does not result in a lost of data, and consequently the application becomes more robust. However, if the system repeatedly loses deadlines, buffers will eventually become full. In other words, the different bottlenecks of the system appear in the form of tasks consistently missing deadlines.

When applying RMA to a real-world data acquisition application, we must be aware of the limitations and assumptions of the basic theory [3,91. In [31 we can find a more realistic formulation of the extended [a, 7.91 rate monotonic test that is useful for testing the schedulability of real-world applications. Unlike the processor utilization time, the time that a task is blocked barely effects other task's schedulability. This is very important for data acquisition applications, because it means that the time that a higher priority task spends performing blocking U 0 does not affect the schedulability of lower priority tasks. We can define X i = Bi + Ii + DEi, where:

Bi includes task's blocking time due to synchronization with lower priority tasks (under the priority ceiling protocol), and due to other sources such as interrupts, etc. Ii is the idle time that a task spends waiting for the completion of all blocking 40 calls that it performs, such as DMA operations. In data acquisition applications this term is usually the most important.

Although the idle time usually benefits lower priority tasks (that can be freely executed during this I D operations), it has two subtle side-effects. First, when a task blocks performing DMA, it steals memory cycles to the other tasks, regardless of their priority. For lower priority tasks, it appears as if the blocked task were using processor time. For higher priority tasks, this situation can be modelled as a priority inversion scenario.

Hopefully, the effect of stealing cycles is minimized by the fact that memory pages accessed by other tasks are likely to reside in the cache. Hence, tasks do not need to access main memory very often and the thread performing DMA barely blocks other higher or lower priority tasks. The extended rate monotonic test from which (EQ 1) is derived is neat and provides a sufficient condition for schedulability. However, it does not provide a necessary condition; in other words, it is too pessimistic. If we manage to defer all the VO operations that a particular task needs to accomplish until the end of its period, and then we perform an asynchronous I/O call, all the idle time of the task occurs after all the non-idle time. The results of the asynchronous I/O can be checked at the beginning of the next period. Under this conditions, there is no deferred execution penalty for lower priority tasks [3]. What is more important, the idle time can now be modelled adding a deadline to the task, instead of adding a blocking factor. This deadline is the latest point in time at which the asynchronous I/O can start within the period, in order to end before the next period begins. Thus, this deadline equals the period minus the duration of the ID operation. For instance (see FIGURE 2), if a task has period of 10 msec., runs for 2 msec. and then performs an asynchronous I/O read that lasts 6 msec., it has a deadline at time 4 msec., because if the non-idle time of the task ends after that instant, the asynchronous 1/0 will finish after the beginning of the next period.

This model that we are proposing is much less restrictive than considering asynchronous I/O idle time as an extra blocking factor, as we did in (EQ 1) and (EQ 2). div.head: Development methodology
div.p: The inequalities given in the previous Section are easy to compute for a real-world application if the engineer proceeds systematically. The analysis can be carried out in four steps:

Construction of the schedulability model. The first goal is to find C'j and Xi for each task, and to mathematically characterize their timing behavior. In our example application we built many different schedulability models as our understanding of the system under development was increasing. However, in the early stages of the development of a system it is often impossible to have an exact characterization of how long does it take to execute a task. In our example system we estimated the length of tasks by guessing on the values of the different terms in the equations.

Experimental measures of some subsystems. As some hardware subsystems become available and interconnected, experimental measures of performance should be done. (Unfortunately, they often can not be accomplished until quite late in the development phase).

In our example system, we made performance measures as soon as we had the reflective memory and the bus adaptor installed. Later in the development process, we were able to fully characterize the system in terms of worst-case execution time. We did not use any tool for finding the actual figures, but rather we made experimental measures under worst-case conditions.

Scbedulability analysis. The next step consists in integrating the experimental measures in the different schedulability tests. If any task is not schedulable, we can benefit from the mathematical characterization of the system that has been made in previous steps to find the reasons for non-schedulabiity.

Unlike expected, the exact numbers pointed out that the problem was not an excessive idle time waiting for DMA completion, but rather what happened was that the execution time was much longer than estimated previously. Looking again at the equations, we found two main reasons for this long execution time: the operating system and driver overhead for setting up DMA operations ( K D ~) , and the context switching latency (CJ.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper we have investigated the application of rate manotonic theory to data acquisition applications. in the context of pushing the different technologies to their hardware and software limits. Our god was to show the utility of the results of R M A to analyze real-world applications that, for instance, cany out DMA operations and suffer the operating system overhead for conbxt switching.

Besides. we have proposed a modelling paradigm for tasks that perform asynchronous I D at the end of its period. These tasks can be modelled as having a deadline at the point in which the I. IO operation should start in order to finish before the next period of the task.

BeneetsofRMA.Our focussing on an example application developed at the CeSATlab of the UAM has allowed us to stress some of the benefits of RMA. From our practical experience, we can highlight the following:
The most obvious asset of this analysis is that it allows to predict the schedulability of a set of tasks.

Moreover, it forces the designer to mathematically characterize the timing behavior of hidher application. This is exmmely useful when looking for application bottlenecks and when choosing the optimization for code if it fails to meet the timing specifications.

It also helps to understand the operating system overhead and to find ways to minimize it (for instance, reducing the number of idle time sections in a periodic t a w Additionally, it allows the designer to fully understand the limitations of an existing system and to evaluate the impact of new technological breakthroughs.
LmitationsofRMA.There are also some limitations in the theory:

The designer needs to estimate the terms due to intempt blocking and non-preemption areas of the operating system. This can be a tough job even in systems running hard real time operating systems and with few tasks and interrupt sources.
Besides. tasks performing DMA steal memory cycles to other tasks regardless of its priority. The exact characterization of this effect is probably beyond the scope of most development projects.

Another important limitation of this analysis is that it can not be fully canid out until an advanced point in the development phase. This is specially true for heterogeneous applications built with the latest technology. Hence, design errors are found out when it is expensive to correct them. For this reason, it is important to early estimate the duration of tasks and blocking sections of code, and to make experimental measures of the different subsystems as soon as they become operative.

Finally, and as it is pointed out in 111, the schedulability tests tend to be too pessimistic, specially in applications in which the amount of code written to cope with exceptions and other atypical scenarios is considerable large. In our application this was not the case, and we believe that it is always desirable to leave some processor time free just in case any unaccounted effect takes place. In data acquisition applications, this extra security can be obtained by having tasks read buffers well before they become full. In this manner, a transient missed deadline does not result in a lost of data.
